name: Liam Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Liam. I work as a field researcher for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and this conversation is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a hospital extension for a firm called Northgate Civils, on the formwork gang. Formwork is the timber and plywood moulds you build so concrete can be poured into the shape of a wall or a floor. I cut ply, carry props, oil the forms, and after the pour I help strike them, which means take them down and clean them for the next one. The proper carpenters do the clever setting out, I'm the junior who does a lot of lifting and a bit of building.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove a delivery van for twenty-two years. By the end the route software timed my every stop, down to the second, and I thought, I'm fifty, I want to make something I can point at. My brother-in-law knew the gang boss, Stan, so I started labouring and I've been learning ever since. Eight years in and I'm still the junior, because I started from nothing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like pour days, when the truck turns up and the concrete fills a form we built, and it holds. It's a good feeling, a bit nervy. What's hard is the cold in January and the fact that my hands don't remember things as fast as the young ones' do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, it's another fad, like the 3D printed houses they were promising ten years back. I'd say it in the canteen and maybe on the family group chat. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. June and I have five years left on the mortgage and I'd like to work to sixty-six. If nothing big changes, that plan holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now: work, overtime when it's there, overpay the mortgage by a hundred a month. We've got about three months in savings and I'd keep that as our rainy-day pot. Maybe I'd do my formwork ticket next year, the course that lets you set out on your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quietly glad, like a pour that goes off without a leak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the formwork course. What's stopped you so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nerves about the written part. I left school at fifteen. The young lad, Josh, said he'd help me revise, and June says I'm making excuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I asked one about how much pressure wet concrete puts on a form, to check I understood Stan. And June uses it to plan our holidays, cheaper flights and that. It's handy, not life-changing.

S0.say: I'd say it's another fad, like the 3D-printed houses promised ten years ago. I'd mention it in the canteen and on the family group chat, nothing dramatic.
S0.think: Privately it's fine for me, with five years left on the mortgage and a plan to work to sixty-six. If nothing big changes, that plan holds.
S0.do: Keeps working on the formwork gang with overtime when it comes, and overpays the mortgage by a hundred a month. Keeps three months of savings as a rainy-day pot and plans to take the formwork ticket next year.
S0.feel: Calm and quietly glad, like a pour with no leaks.
S0.quote: Quietly glad, like a pour that goes off without a leak.
S0.fieldNote: Liam is measured and steady, with a clear retirement plan built around the mortgage. He uses AI occasionally and sees it as handy rather than life-changing. His fear of the written exam is a small, human gap in an otherwise calm picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some things will change and some won't, and it's not worth getting worked up. Formwork has already gone half to steel systems that click together, and we survived that. That's what I'd tell the gang.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit worried about my end of the job. The lifting and cleaning and cutting are the easiest parts to give to a machine, and the setting out is where the skill is. So I need to get to the skilled end before the machine gets to my end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the formwork ticket this year, not next, and ask Stan to let me set out with the laser level. I'd get Josh to show me the app the engineers use for drawings, now I've seen others use it. And I'd keep overpaying the mortgage so it's done sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a get-on-with-it way. Like a sore back you know you need to stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the gang would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stan, oddly. He's the best formwork carpenter I know, but he's sixty-two and hates screens. If the drawings all go on tablets, he'd struggle, and I'd hate to see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said both "it's not worth getting worked up" and that you need to move fast. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. In public you keep calm, so the young ones don't panic. In private you get your skates on.

S1.say: I'd tell the gang some things change and some don't, and it's not worth getting worked up. Formwork already went half to click-together steel systems, and we survived.
S1.think: Privately I'd worry about my end of the job, the lifting, cleaning and cutting, which are easiest to hand to a machine. I need to reach the skilled setting-out end before the machine reaches mine.
S1.do: Takes the formwork ticket this year and asks Stan to let him set out with the laser level. Gets Josh to teach him the engineers' drawing app and keeps overpaying the mortgage.
S1.feel: Uneasy in a get-on-with-it way, like a sore back that needs stretching.
S1.quote: In public you keep calm, so the young ones don't panic. In private you get your skates on.
S1.fieldNote: He openly owns the gap between his calm public line and his quicker private moves. His plan is clear: climb from the lifting end to the skilled setting-out end. He picks up tech once he's seen others use it, which fits him exactly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a grown-up plan from the government, fast, whatever party is in. I'm not one for marches, but I'd write to the paper or sign a petition. And I'd tell people at work to sort out their money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a real worry. I'd be sixty, still on the junior end, and June works in a pharmacy, where a machine can count pills better than anyone. But we've got the house, and that's our way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sell the house and buy a smaller place outright, probably a flat near our daughter Hana on the coast, so no mortgage at all. I'd stop the overpaying and keep every penny as cash instead. We'd cut back hard, no holiday, no new van for Ben's birthday surprise we'd been planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a big knot in my stomach. But I'd have a plan by the weekend, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would June feel about selling the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd cry, the kids grew up there. Then she'd start clearing the loft the next day, because that's June. We've talked about downsizing before, just not this soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for income once you're there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe small jobs, or nothing. If robots do it all, maybe there's a government payment, but I wouldn't bet the house on it, I'd have already sold it.

S2.say: I'd say this needs a grown-up plan from the government, fast, whichever party is in. I'm not a marcher, but I'd sign a petition and tell people at work to sort their money out.
S2.think: Privately it's a real worry: I'd be sixty, still junior, and June's pharmacy job could go to a machine. But we own most of the house, and that's our way out.
S2.do: Sells the house and buys a smaller flat outright near their daughter on the coast, ending the mortgage. Stops overpaying and keeps the cash instead, and cuts back hard on holidays and planned gifts.
S2.feel: Anxious with a knot in his stomach, steadied by having a plan by the weekend.
S2.quote: I wouldn't bet the house on it, I'd have already sold it.
S2.fieldNote: What keeps him from full alarm is home equity, which gives him a real option. He's honest that he has no idea how he'd earn afterwards. June's reaction, crying then clearing the loft, sums up the household's practical streak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people start now. I'd say it to the gang: get your money straight, don't buy that new truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years means I could clear the mortgage before it hits, if we push hard. I'd be sixty-three and debt-free, and that changes everything. It's tight but doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd double the mortgage overpayments, two hundred a month, and take every Saturday shift going. I'd get my ticket so I'm useful as long as possible. And June and I would plan to stop at sixty-three instead of sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's the kind of worry you can work off. I like a target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you have to give up to double the overpayments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The season ticket at the football, which hurts. And Saturdays with June, which hurts more. We'd say it's only for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still sell the house, like in the fast picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not straight away. With five years I'd rather clear it and keep it. If things got bad, we'd sell then, but on our terms, not in a panic.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people start now. I'd tell the gang to get their money straight and not buy that new truck.
S3.think: Privately five years means I could clear the mortgage before it hits. Being sixty-three and debt-free changes everything, tight but doable.
S3.do: Doubles mortgage overpayments to two hundred a month and takes every Saturday shift. Gets his formwork ticket to stay useful, and plans with June to stop at sixty-three.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but the kind of worry he can work off with a target.
S3.quote: If things got bad, we'd sell then, but on our terms, not in a panic.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him keep the house and simply finish the mortgage early. His whole approach is about targets and control. Giving up Saturdays with June bothers him more than the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up, and people who don't plan will only have themselves to blame, mostly. Though I'd say the government should help the ones who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's nearly the plan we already had. Sixty-eight in 2036, mortgage gone, two years retired. It would be the kids and grandkids I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal, do my ticket, keep overpaying at the usual rate. I'd probably say to Ben, who's a plumber, to keep an eye on what robots can do in his trade. Nothing drastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's like hearing the storm will hit after you've moved house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ben?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, son, you've got time, use it. Learn the systems, the boilers that think for themselves, be the one who fixes them. He'd say he's already on it, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said people will mostly have themselves to blame. Is that fair on someone like Stan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, you're right, it isn't. Stan's not lazy, he just won't take to screens. That's what I meant about the ones who can't.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up and people who don't plan mostly have themselves to blame. But the government should help those who can't.
S4.think: Privately it's nearly the plan we had: sixty-eight in 2036, mortgage gone and two years retired. My thoughts would go to the kids and grandkids.
S4.do: Carries on as normal, takes his ticket and keeps overpaying the mortgage at the usual rate. Encourages his son Ben, a plumber, to learn the new automated systems.
S4.feel: Calm, like hearing a storm will hit after you've moved house.
S4.quote: Stan's not lazy, he just won't take to screens.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his original plan works unchanged. When challenged on blaming people, he softened it straight away for his colleague Stan, which shows his centrist, fair-minded side. His concern shifts to his son's trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. We'd have to sell the house in a rush, and June's job would go too. What would help is some kind of bridge payment until the state pension, and a straight answer from the government early, so you can plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the house. Everyone talks about jobs, but for people my age the house is what decides whether you're fine or not. If you rent at sixty, a robot taking your job is a different story.

headlineQuote: If you rent at sixty, a robot taking your job is a different story.
portrait: Liam is a fifty-eight-year-old former delivery driver who joined a formwork gang on a hospital extension eight years ago and is still the junior doing the lifting and cleaning. He's measured and fair-minded, uses AI tools now and then, and plans everything around paying off his mortgage. Steady change pushes him to climb towards the skilled setting-out work. Two-year AGI makes him anxious but not lost, because selling the house is a real way out, while five years lets him clear the mortgage and ten years leaves his plan intact.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because they'd have to sell the house in a rush and June's pharmacy job would go too.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge payment until the state pension, and clear answers from the government early enough to plan.
